transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2027-10-10 16:30 UTC
Duration: 48 minutes (approx)
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Diego Ramos (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (Redwood Product), Evan Park (Glacier Head of Platform), Sofia Li (ML Eng), Daniel Ortiz (Security)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be rough):
- Demo of Redwood Optimize console heuristics and KV/prefix cache recommendations.
- Walked through cost model tradeoffs between batching and prefetching; showed sandbox numbers.
- Customer wants pilot with live traces, emphasized security (KMS, audit logs) and latency SLOs for their real-time assistant.

Topics detected:
- Cost models and assumptions
- Batch sizing and concurrency vs latency
- Prefix/KV cache TTLs and eviction strategy
- Routing to Dedicated vs Hosted
- Security (KMS, SSO, audit)

Action items recapped at end (see metadata list)

Transcript body:
00:00 Maya: OK hi everyone thanks for joining, um we'll give a 45-ish minute walkthrough of our Optimize heuristics and specifically how we recommend prefix / KV caching for a low-latency assistant workload. Diego and Priya from our team will demo the console and run a short sandbox sim.
00:18 Evan: Great thanks Maya, appreciate it. We have about 48 minutes, so perfect. Sofia and I will try to jump in with some sample traces we sent earlier.
00:28 Diego: Awesome, I'll start by setting context — quick note, I'm going to reference our Optimizer tab in Console which in some exports shows up as "Redwood Optima" in the logs, that's just an ASR quirk.
00:40 Diego: So high-level, two levers most teams use: batching (to amortize token compute) and prefix/KV caching (to avoid redoing repeated context). We'll show the cost model outputs, then an example plan for Glacier's real-time assistant.
01:05 Sofia: Quick question - our assistant needs 200ms p95 end-to-end, and often the prompt is 256 tokens. Will batching break that?
01:15 Diego: Good call — depends on concurrency patterns. If you get many concurrent single-turn requests, batching can add queueing latency. Our console has a slider for latency SLO and it suggests a batch size distribution that keeps p95 under target.
01:30 Priya: I'll share screen of the Optimize console now — there are three panes: workload profile, cost model, and recommended configs. The workload profile can be fed by sample traces or by our traffic generator.
01:48 (screen share noise)
02:02 Diego: Here's Glacier's sample input (Sofia's traces) plotted — lots of short sessions with repeated system prompts; you can see a spike in prefix reuse which is prime for KV cache.
02:20 Sofia: Yeah that replay is accurate, typically we have 12–18 concurrent users in peak region and lots of similar system prompt tokens.
02:34 Diego: Perfect — so Optimize immediately flags prefetch candidate prefixes. See this table: prefix hit-rate estimate 42% and projected token savings 32% if we prefetch top-20 prefixes into KV cache per session.
02:56 Evan: When you say "prefetch" is that session-level or global? We have multi-tenant concen— uh concern about memory.
03:10 Priya: Good catch — default approach is session-affine prefetching: we keep a per-session small KV-store that holds the user-specific prefix entries. For multi-tenant shared prefixes (like product marketing boilerplates) we have a shared namespace option to avoid duplication.
03:32 Daniel: Security question — where is the KV-stored data encrypted and how is key rotation handled?
03:40 Maya: For Private and Dedicated customers we integrate with your KMS/HSM. For hosted, Redwood uses customer-managed keys via our KMS integration when requested. Rotation policies can be pushed from your KMS and we surface audit logs for all KV reads/writes. We'll attach SOC2 and encryption docs after the call.
04:05 Diego: Back to econ: the cost model shows three paths: aggressive prefetch (bigger memory, fewer tokens), conservative prefetch (smaller memory, moderate savings), and batch-heavy (increase batching to reduce per-token compute). The console outputs expected cost per 1M requests for each path.
04:28 Sofia: Could you show a worked example with our numbers?
04:35 Diego: Sure — switching the cost model inputs to Glacier traces... done. So, baseline hosted no-prefetch and single-threaded service: estimated $X per million tokens (note: dollar values approximated in the sandbox). With session KV prefetch top-20 prefixes and steady batch size 8 at peak concurrency, cost drops ~28% but memory use per-session rises by ~150KB.
05:05 Evan: And latency?
05:09 Diego: p95 improves because fewer tokens are generated (prefix cached), plus batching at size 8 still meets 200ms p95 in this sim. If you increase batch size to 16 you'll save more but risk p95 exceeding 200ms during spikes.
05:30 Priya: One nuance: KV lookup adds a constant ~5–12ms depending on placement (intra-node vs remote). Our runtime prefers co-located KV to keep lookups sub-10ms.
05:45 Sofia: Our infra is hybrid: some requests from EU, some from NA. Does Optimize include region-aware routing suggestions?
05:54 Diego: Yes — we can recommend routing rules. For example, route EU traffic to EU Dedicated pool and use local KV clusters; fallback to hosted in other region. That reduces cross-region RTT and conforms to data residency needs.
06:12 Daniel: About auditability — can we get token-level logs for KV hits/misses without storing user content? We need to redact PII.
06:22 Maya: We have sampling and redaction flags, and our audit pipeline can emit hit/miss metrics and token counts without storing full prompt text. We'll send the compliance playbook after.
06:35 Diego: Now I'll demo adaptive prefetch heuristics. The console supports two modes: threshold-based (prefetch when prefix reuse > X%) and predictive (model-based lookahead that ranks candidate prefixes per session). Predictive takes historical traces to train a light-weight model.
06:55 Sofia: Does predictive require us to share traces? Any privacy concerns?
07:02 Diego: Only aggregated and hashed n-gram features are needed; we can run the trainer inside your VPC (Private) if you want — so raw text never leaves.
07:12 Priya: I'll toggle predictive on for Glacier traces. You can see the hit-rate projection improve from 42% to 58% for the top-30 prefixes after one training pass.
07:30 Evan: Nice, that seems meaningful. How stable are these predictions for seasonal content?
07:38 Diego: We support periodic re-training and TTLs; we recommend weekly retrain for churny domains. For very stable content monthly is fine.
07:50 Sofia: On eviction — are prefixes evicted by LRU or TTL? We have some prefixes that are large but low utility.
07:58 Diego: We support hybrid policies: TTL + size threshold + LRU. In Console you can set max memory per session and eviction policy; Optimize will simulate resulting hit-rates and cost.
08:14 Priya: Here's the simulate button — running scenario 1: session prefetch top-20, TTL 24h, max per-session mem 1MB... running...
08:26 (short wait)
08:30 Diego: Results: hit-rate 51%, projected token savings 27%, added mem overhead cluster-wide estimate 120GB at your QPS. Cost per-hour delta is shown here.
08:44 Evan: 120GB at QPS — is that across Dedicated or within Hosted?
08:50 Priya: That's across the Dedicated pool if you choose Dedicated. If you choose Hosted, we estimate a different memory footprint because we shard KV differently. Console shows both variants.
09:06 Daniel: And what about fallback policies? If KV misses or cache node fails do we gracefully fallback to smaller model or different region?
09:16 Diego: Yep the runtime supports graceful fallback: fallback routes to a compatible model variant or a lower-latency replica. You can set fallback to "serve-without-prefetch" which avoids tail latencies when KV is down.
09:28 Maya: At this point, I want to call out the cost vs latency frontier. Optimize exposes a slider: lower cost => larger batching and more aggressive quantization; lower latency => smaller batches and more local KV. You tune based on your SLO and budget.
09:50 Evan: Quantization — are you recommending int8 for our model? We worried about quality drift.
09:57 Priya: For many workloads int8 is sensible. Optimize will run a quick eval on your prompt set (we ran it earlier on a subset) and show quality delta. For Glacier's prompts, int8 had negligible BLEU-like metric change but we can share the eval report.
10:16 Sofia: Did you test for hallucination or safety regressions?
10:22 Diego: We run regression tests on critical prompts and have a risk score tied to evaluation sets. We can include a safety checklist in the pilot.
10:30 Evan: On Dedicated vs Hosted — for a pilot which path makes more sense?
10:36 Maya: For quick time-to-value, starting hosted with Optimize sandbox is fastest; it gives console recommendations and you can run a 1-week pilot. If you need strict isolation and KMS/HSM integration, Dedicated or Private is recommended. We often run a hosted pilot and then switch to Dedicated when commit is needed.
10:58 Daniel: Security/contract Q — do you support SAML SSO and SCIM for provisioning?
11:04 Maya: Yes, SAML SSO and SCIM are supported for orgs. We'll include the SSO integration guide in the followup.
11:12 Priya: Back to numbers — Diego will show a microbenchmark comparing batch sizes on our runtimes.
11:20 Diego: I'm going to run a live microbench: single-turn 256 tokens baseline, batch sizes 1,4,8,16 measured on gpu-x1 in sandbox. Note this is a demo cluster; hardware may vary.
11:36 (benchmark run sounds)
12:00 Diego: Results (approx): batch1 avg latency 72ms per request, batch4 58ms, batch8 73ms (queueing creep), batch16 120ms. So you see a sweet spot at 4 for this seq length on this hardware. The cost-per-token goes down with larger batches but at batch8 latency rises due to queueing under this request pattern.
12:29 Sofia: Interesting batch8 got worse than batch4 here. Is that due to token distribution?
12:36 Diego: Yes, because our request inter-arrival distribution is bursty. If traffic were more uniform batch8 could be optimal. Optimize will simulate with your real traces to find optimal batch target and concurrency.
12:51 Priya: Let's demo an end-to-end recommended config for Glacier: session-affine KV prefetch top-25, TTL 12h, predictive lookahead on, batch target 4, concurrency cap 24, fallback to smaller model on failure. This config projects 26% cost savings and keeps p95 < 200ms.
13:18 Evan: That projection assumes X% uptime for KV cluster, right?
13:24 Diego: We assume 99.9% KV availability in the model; you can slide that parameter. If KV availability drops to 99% cost savings drop by ~6% and tail latencies increase; console will flag that.
13:41 Sofia: For the pilot, we want to test on a Dedicated pool with co-located KV. Can you outline what Redwood needs from us?
13:52 Maya: Sure — we'll need: 1) 7 days of sample traces (anonymized) or live stream, 2) target SLOs and success criteria, 3) contact for infra access if you want Dedicated/private, and 4) decision timeline.
14:10 Evan: Decision timeline — we aim for an infra decision by end of Q4. Pilot should help.
14:18 Priya: Diego, can you pull the sandbox sim results into a CSV for Evan?
14:22 Diego: Yes will export and share.
14:25 (brief side chatter)
15:00 Daniel: Quick compliance nit: egress constraints — some prefixes contain PII in our logs, we need to ensure redaction pre-ingest. Is there a recommended pipeline?
15:12 Maya: Yes — we have a pre-ingest connector that can be deployed in your VPC to redact PII and hash tokens before sending to Redwood Optimize. We'll send the connector config.
15:28 Sofia: About instrumentation — what's needed in our app to support session-level affinity?
15:34 Diego: You just need a stable session id in the request header; Console will show session heatmaps. If you can't provide that, we can use request fingerprinting but it's less accurate.
15:44 Evan: Any major hidden costs we should watch for? For example, KV memory, network egress, and longer model context windows?
15:52 Priya: The big ones are KV memory and higher storage for cached prefixes; network egress for cross-region lookups; and extra compute if you keep larger context windows. Optimize shows a breakdown so you can see which line items drive cost.
16:10 Sofia: About model routing — can we route long-context requests to a different variant that has larger kv and smaller batch?
16:18 Diego: Yep that's a common pattern: long-context goes to a large model variant with aggressive prefix caching; short queries go to smaller variant optimized for latency. Console can synthesize routing policies.
16:30 Priya: We're approaching the demo wrap-up; final part I'll flip to the pilot checklist and timeline.
16:39 (screen share flip)
16:45 Priya: Pilot checklist on screen: traces, SLOs, pilot duration 7–14 days, success metric (token cost reduction >=20% and p95 <=200ms). Also notes on security gates: SOC2, KMS integration, SAML SSO.
16:59 Evan: That seems fair. We prefer 7 days initially.
17:05 Maya: Great. Quick recap of next steps: Maya will send pricing and the pilot contract; Diego will export benchmark CSV and a recommended config JSON (note - JSON link will be in email); Priya will attach SOC2 and the compliance playbook; Sofia will send the traces.
17:25 Daniel: One last question — what about failure modes for prefetch poisoning (malicious prefixes)? Do you detect anomalous prefix patterns?
17:36 Diego: We have anomaly detection rules for prefix churn and weird frequency spikes. We can disable predictive prefetching for sessions that fail sanity checks. We'll provide the ruleset.
17:50 Evan: OK good. Thanks everyone — this was really helpful.
17:57 Maya: Thanks all — we'll follow up with the artifacts.
18:03 Sofia: Thanks, bye.
18:08 (call ends)

Post-call notes (auto):
- Customer interested in Dedicated pilot with co-located KV to meet 200ms p95 SLO.
- Key followups: cost-model spreadsheet, SOC2 and KMS docs, exported benchmark CSV, pilot config.
- Risk/objection: memory overhead and multi-tenant duplication; suggested mitigation: shared namespace for common prefixes and conservative TTL.

End of transcript
